title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a music-generation system trained on copyrighted recordings without obtaining licenses from the rights holders before deployment. Udio launched publicly and attracted millions of users while that training-data question remained unresolved. The failure happened at the data-preparation stage, before the model was ever made available, and catching it would have required a rights-clearance review of the training corpus prior to ingestion.

The legal landscape that followed is complex. Universal Music Group settled and entered a licensing arrangement with Udio. Warner Music Group did the same. Sony Music filed at least two separate lawsuits, with one alleging use of more than 30,000 recordings; a judge barred Sony from adding those recordings to its original case, after which Sony filed a new action to assert them separately. A copyright class action brought by independent artists was not dismissed and was transferred to New York. A musicians' union also filed suit over the UMG settlement itself, and UMG has asked a court to dismiss that claim.

None of the lawsuits has produced a final verdict on the underlying copyright question, and the allegations of infringement are not yet findings of fact. What is established is that Udio trained on music whose copyright status relative to the training use was disputed, that two major labels resolved their disputes through licensing deals rather than judicial rulings, and that additional litigation from Sony and from independent artists remains active.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve claims that Udio used copyrighted music to train its artificial intelligence system. The settlement includes Udio's commitment to launch a new platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs. UMG had accused Udio of generating music similar to copyrighted hits like The Temptations' "My Girl," but the companies did not disclose the financial terms of the deal.

This settlement marks Udio's first major licensing agreement with a major music label. Udio's CEO expressed enthusiasm about collaborating with UMG to create tools that support artists and fans. The company plans to compensate artists who opt into the new platform, though specific details remain undisclosed. Udio, launched in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, has attracted millions of users since its release and counts music artist will.i.am among its backers.
